ledger.sentence: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density.
ledger.note: Title of ROS page; textbook expansion.

ledger.sentence: The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker.
The NHS lists DEXA among the tests that use X-rays.
ledger.note: NHS X-ray page: DEXA for bone density.

ledger.sentence: NHS 111 Wales says a scan may be offered to people over 50 who are at risk of osteoporosis.
It also says people under 50 may be offered one if they have other risk factors, such as smoking or a previous broken bone.
A doctor usually makes the referral.
Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.
The person lies on their back on a padded table.
A scanning arm passes over the body, usually the hips and spine, and the images go to a computer.
The scan is painless and takes between about 5 and 15 minutes, depending on the sources and the body part scanned.
The dose is low.
A Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small and says there are no side effects of bone density scanning.
The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
Scores fall into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis, and the laboratory report shows the bands used.
Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip.
The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.
A T-score does not decide treatment alone.
The Royal Osteoporosis Society says the decision to offer a medicine is based on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, rather than only on bone density.
A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a padded table while a scanning arm passes over the hips and spine.
The radiation dose is low, and a Royal Marsden leaflet describes the added risk as extremely small.
The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
The decision to offer a medicine rests on the overall chance of breaking a bone in the next ten years, not on the scan result alone.
A DXA scan measures bone density at the hip and spine using very low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who is offered one and what the T-score does and does not decide.
